prompt.en: In the practical radio-horizon model, one antenna is raised from 16 m to 64 m. What happens to that antenna's own horizon contribution?

text.en: It doubles, because square root of height rises from 4 to 8.

feedback.en: The model uses square root of height, not height itself. The other station's contribution is separate.

text.en: It becomes four times larger because height becomes four times larger.

feedback.en: That treats horizon as directly proportional to height and ignores the square root.

text.en: It is unchanged unless transmitter power rises too.

feedback.en: The height term changes even at unchanged power.

text.en: The whole two-station path necessarily becomes twice as long.

feedback.en: Only this antenna's contribution doubles. Add the other station's unchanged contribution before comparing total path estimates.

explanation.en: Separate the changed antenna contribution from the combined path, and remember that terrain can still limit coverage.

prompt.en: A steady VHF path opens along a lake inversion while an HF sky-wave route is poor. Are those observations contradictory?

text.en: Yes; good VHF propagation proves the same F-region conditions must support HF.

feedback.en: The VHF weather-layer path and HF ionospheric path depend on different regions.

text.en: No; lower-atmosphere conditions can improve VHF independently of the ionospheric HF route.

feedback.en: A tropospheric enhancement does not establish a useful F-region path at the planned HF frequency.

text.en: Yes; an inversion must improve every frequency by the same amount.

feedback.en: A weather structure is not a universal gain increase across all bands and paths.

text.en: No; both observations prove that all VHF openings are sporadic E.

feedback.en: The lake inversion points to a lower-atmosphere mechanism, not an automatic E-region explanation.

explanation.en: Interpret the band and physical region together. An opening on one path does not prove that another band is open.

prompt.en: Weak smeared HF fragments are heard inside an area usually skipped by the main sky-wave return. What conclusion is justified?

text.en: The main return point must have moved to that area, making ordinary message service dependable.

feedback.en: Weak scattered fragments do not establish a new reliable main return.

text.en: The receiver must be faulty because a skip zone can never contain any energy.

feedback.en: Scatter can redirect a small part of the signal into an area missed by the main path.

text.en: Scattered energy may be reaching the area without creating a reliable main-hop path.

feedback.en: Only a small fraction may arrive over irregular paths, explaining weak and smeared copy.

text.en: The signal must be a surface ground wave because it is closer than the main return.

feedback.en: Location alone does not establish ground wave. The weakness and smearing can fit scatter.

explanation.en: A skip zone describes the main coverage gap, not a rule that absolutely no scattered energy can arrive there.
